g: (Greek mythology) Of or relating to Iacchus.

A Japanese martial art associated with the smooth, controlled movements of drawing the sword from its scabbard, striking or cutting an opponent, removing blood from the blade, and then replacing the sword in the scabbard.
(prosody) A metrical foot in verse consisting of an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable.
(prosody) A verse consisting of an iambic dimeter and half an elegiac pentameter.
(prosody) Consisting of iambs (metrical feet with an unstressed–stressed pattern) or characterized by their predominance. [from 16th c.]
(prosody) An iamb; a line or group of lines of iambs.
A poetic meter consisting of lines with five iambic feet each, meaning the even syllables are dominant.

(prosody) In Latin, the shortening of an etymologically long final vowel, in a two-syllable word where the first vowel is also short. It tended to persist in uninflected words like bene, but was levelled out in favour of inflectional regularity in other words.
A poetic meter consisting of lines with four iambic feet each, meaning the even syllable is dominant.
One who writes in iambic meter.
A poet who writes iambic verse.
(Ancient Greece) A member of an Olympian dynasty, the "house of Iamus", an extended family of seers.
Any porifer of the family Ianthellidae
Any of the family Epitoniidae (syn. Janthinidae) of violet snails.
(mineralogy) An orthorhombic-pyramidal mineral containing hydrogen, oxygen, and uranium.
(mythology) Of or relating to the Titan Iapetus in Greek mythology.
(astronomy) Of or relating to the Saturnian moon Iapetus, named for the Titan god.
(historical) An ancient people who dwelt north of and inland from the Liburnians, off the Adriatic coast and eastwards of the Istrian peninsula.

(historical) A member of an Indo-European-speaking people, dwelling in Iapygia (modern Apulia) in the southeastern Italian Peninsula between the beginning of the first millennium BC and the first century BC. They were divided into three tribes: the Daunians, Peucetians, and Messapians.
Of or pertaining to the Iatmul people.
An ethnic group of people inhabiting some two dozen autonomous villages along the middle Sepik River in Papua New Guinea.
(medicine) Pertaining to the application of remedies by rubbing, especially by rubbing in oil or balm.
Of or pertaining to a physician or physicians.
(chemistry, medicine) An early branch of chemistry, having roots in alchemy, that tried to provide chemical remedies to diseases; alternatively, the application of chemistry to medical theory.
The act of killing a patient by medical treatment.
A large-scale problem caused by a medical procedure or drug.
The drug thalidomide caused many birth defects and led to an iatroepidemic.
(medicine) Any adverse effect (or complication) resulting from medical treatment.
(medicine, of a disease, injury, or other adverse outcome) Induced by the words or actions of the physician or by medical treatment or diagnostic procedure.
Someone who studies iatromathematics; a physician applying a mathematical theory of medicine.
A 17th-century Italian doctrine that attempted to apply the laws of mechanics and mathematics to the human body.
(historical, medicine) Describing a school of thought that maintained that physiology and pathology could be explained in terms of physics.
(historical) A proponent of the iatromechanical theory.
(historical) An approach to medical treatment based on chemistry.
An intense dislike of doctors or the medical profession.
An adverse reaction to a prescribed drug or to a medical procedure
A person who has iatrophobia; one who fears going to the doctor.
An abnormal or irrational fear of doctors or going to the doctor.
(medicine) Of or relating to a 17th-century school of medical thought that explained all physiological and pathological phenomena by the laws of physics; opposed to the iatrochemical school.
(historical, medicine) A physician who was a follower of iatrophysics.
(medicine) Causing a patient to need medical attention, especially when caused by a medical treatment.
(by extension) Pertaining to professional attention or opinions that cause the need for further professional attention or opinions.
(dated, medicine, surgery, rare) The art of medicine and surgery
That seeks surgery or medical attention (for nonmedical reasons)
(historical) A tribe of Sarmatia settled on the Danube.
(Lovecraftian) An interjection for summoning an outer deity, glossed over as a cry for food.
